messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Karl's Vigilance

Karl was seventy-four when the hurricane came. He had lived in Charleston for forty-three years—long enough to know which storms were bluster and which were real. Hurricane Marcus was real. On the afternoon it made landfall, he and his wife Elena had sheltered in place in their house on King Street, a decision that had seemed reasonable at the time. The wind came in waves, each one louder than the last, and then the water followed. It rose through the first floor with a speed that made thought impossible. Karl remembered the smell—a thick, acrid mix of seawater and whatever chemicals had been torn loose from the industrial district upstream—and the sound of it, a kind of roar that seemed to come from everywhere at once. He remembered Elena's hand in his, and then he remembered being separated from her by the current, his body slammed against the kitchen counter, the water filling his mouth and nose. He had pulled himself upward by instinct alone, gasping, finding the stairwell, climbing. The water had stopped rising at the second-floor landing. He had waited there for hours, unable to move, unable to think, until the rescue team found him. Elena had made it to the roof. They were both alive.

But something in Karl had not come back down from that landing.

In the months that followed, he had found himself unable to sit comfortably in any room without knowing exactly what was behind him. At the tutoring center where he worked three afternoons a week—a converted brownstone on Broad Street where he helped high school students with their essays—he would position himself at the corner desk, back to the wall, eyes on the door and the room beyond it. His students noticed. One of them, a quiet girl named Maya, had asked if he was okay. He had said yes, of course, but the question had lodged itself in his mind. Was he okay? The honest answer was that he felt unsafe unless he could see everything, unless he could anticipate what might come. When a lesson ran longer than scheduled, or when a student arrived late, or when Elena took longer than expected at the grocery store, Karl's mind would leap to catastrophe. Something bad was happening. Something was always about to happen. He found himself scanning the tutoring center obsessively—the fire exits, the windows, the structural integrity of the walls. He would notice a crack in the plaster and imagine it widening, water pouring through. He would hear a siren and assume it was coming for him.

The memories made it worse. Sometimes, without warning, the afternoon of the hurricane would force itself into his mind while he was working with a student. He would be reviewing an essay about climate change, and suddenly he would smell it—that chemical-seawater smell—and his body would go rigid. Other times, he could recall the event with perfect clarity but feel nothing at all, as if he were watching a film about someone else's drowning, someone else's terror. This strange numbness was almost worse than the intrusive moments, because it made him feel hollow, disconnected even from his own survival. The memories came unbidden and stayed, and each time they did, his conviction that danger was imminent would spike. He had come to believe that his constant vigilance—the scanning, the positioning, the threat assessment—was the only thing keeping him and Elena safe. If he stopped watching, if he let his guard down for even a moment, the next disaster would find him unprepared.

So he had begun to avoid anything that might stress him. He had cut back his tutoring hours, telling his supervisor his arthritis was acting up. He had stopped attending the book club Elena loved. He had declined invitations from friends. Staying home, staying still, staying vigilant—these felt like the only reasonable choices. But the avoidance had its own cost. The less he engaged with the world, the more his mind circled back to the hurricane, the more he ruminated about what he could have done differently, should have done. If only they had evacuated. If only he had moved faster. If only he had held Elena's hand tighter. The rumination fed the memories, which fed the threat-scanning, which fed the avoidance, which left him with nothing but time to ruminate again. Elena had begun to worry aloud. She had asked him to see someone, to talk to a therapist. For months he had resisted, but last week, sitting in the tutoring center with his back to the wall, watching the door, waiting for the next disaster that felt inevitable, he had finally called.
